title: I spent the night in one of Britain's most haunted prisons – now a luxury hotel
excerpt: Once home to murderers, thieves and condemned prisoners, Cornwall's Bodmin Jail has been transformed into a spectacular luxury hotel – but some say its former inmates have never left.
content:
I spent the night in Britain's most haunted hotel - the former prison of Bodmin Moor

Once home to murderers, thieves and condemned prisoners, Cornwall's Bodmin Jail has been transformed into a spectacular luxury hotel – but some say its former inmates have never left.

08:00, 15 Oct 2026Updated 11:47, 15 Oct 2026

Bodmin Jail is the most haunted building in the country by some reckoning, which might make it hard to imagine a peaceful night’s sleep there, but I had three out of three. It’s one of the most exciting places I’ve ever stayed. I expected to walk into something that felt like a hotel, and to find small clues to its old jail status, but no. You walk directly into the main wing, immediately surrounded by the gangways and cells, like a lag. It’s startling, and thrilling. It’s also incredibly plush. Eighteenth-century jail it might be, but this is not hard time.

Sleeping behind bars at Bodmin Jail

My room was made up of three old cells. Two were opened up to create a larger room with a big comfy bed and ultra-soft sheets. The old curved cell ceilings still have the original stone arches, and greeting you as you enter is a small picture and biography of one of the unlucky lags to have slept here before you. Ours was George Trethewy, who found himself on the wrong side of the law after selling his wife at the local market. For clarity, that was not the crime, but he got fourpence for her and refused to hand over the penny fee to the market foreman, and was incarcerated for his trouble.

In the third cell is the bathroom, a boutique masterpiece of exposed stonework and marble, with a huge waterfall shower, huge fluffy white towels and - the piece de resistance - a standalone stone bath. Bathing in an old cell, in rampant luxury, is juxtaposition not to be missed.

If spook is your thing, request Room 311 - the most haunted one in the place (apart from Cell 4 in the basement, which remains locked at all times). Sitting directly above the Condemned Cell, where the 55 executees spent their final hours before the short walk to the long drop noose, knockings, murmurs and ghostly apparitions are frequently reported. Next door in Room 310, I slept like a baby.

Fine dining in the prison chapel

The Chapel Restaurant is, as you would expect, the old chapel of the prison. It’s the only place inmates were allowed to talk (this was a silent jail), so it’s lovely to see it in the buzz of a breakfast service, with the two pulpits decorated with flowers instead of prison guards. Breakfast was generous and delicious - fruit, exceptionally chocolatey chocolate croissants, jams, yoghurt and cheeses, plus a varied list of hot options to choose from, from which I can vouch for the cinnamon porridge (nothing like gruel), the eggs Benedict and the salmon-and-caviar bagel.

At dinner, the emphasis is on Cornish flavours - fish (north or south, you’re only about 10 miles to the sea, here), meat from local farms and seasonal vegetables, with everything beautifully presented on plates subtly adorned with a chain motif (honestly, the little details here are so delightful). I can also recommend Sunday lunch, of which they’re rightly proud, and the pretty afternoon teas where the sandwiches and miniature cakes come in a little tiered cell.

Leave space after dinner for a tipple in The Champagne Bar. The old Governor's quarters, it’s a great place to compare ghost stories with the barman – or other guests – and the cocktails are expert.

Ghost hunts and grisly history

You will want to visit the Jail Attraction while you’re here - it’s on the same site, and it’s impressively well done, with not a dusty mannequin in sight. In the intro, a ghostly warden materialises from a smoke wisp in front of your eyes, and the history of incarcerated women, including Sarah Polgrean, a victim of domestic abuse who poisoned her violent husband, and children as young as six who were locked up, is chilling.

There are three levels of ghostly encounters you can book too, from an evening ghost walk (£30), a ghost hunt that lasts until 2am (£55) to a full-on paranormal investigation overnight in the cells (£75), see Ghost Experiences.

Bodmin itself is not the most enchanting town, but it is brilliantly set for everything that Cornwall offers. Twenty minutes away is the peerless Eden Project - those famous domes of rainforest walks with a tall waterfall and a high lookout platform. Adults £35.50, kids £12.50 and under-5s are free.

What to see near Bodmin Jail

In the other direction, Bodmin Moor is one of Britain’s grand wildernesses, with wild ponies, ancient cairns and mystical glades where you can spot otters in the clattering streams.

Northward, Port Isaac is the village where Doc Martin is set, while nearby Polzeath is a surfing mecca. King Arthur’s Castle at Tintagel is less than 45 minutes away, too. To the south, there are charming fishing villages like Charlestown, Mevagissy and Polperro, where you are constantly faced with that Cornish conundrum of whether to eat fish and chips, crab sandwiches, ice creams or cream teas. Here are some recommendations for each:

Where to eat in Cornwall:

Fish & chips:

  • The Fish Grill, Mevagissy for the trio of fish (haddock, mackerel and scallops) or the haddock bap.
  • Seasmiths Fish & Chips for award-winning eat in or takeaway options, far superior to the flashy offerings down the road in Padstow

Crab sandwiches:

  • All Aboard, Port Isaac for fresh and deeply filled sandwiches

Cream tea:

  • Teacup Tearoom, Mevagissy Enormous scones and acres of clotted cream. I’ve rarely been anywhere they’ve taken the Jam First rule so seriously.
